```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

The openhexa functions take and return plain data frames (tibbles) and files, so they fit with the packages you
already use. This vignette collects short recipes, then puts them together in a complete flow where all the data is
generated in R and OpenHEXA only receives the results.

The recipes assume that you are logged in and a workspace is selected (see `vignette("openhexa")`):

```{r}
library(openhexa)
login(server_url = "https://api.openhexa.org", workspace = "my-workspace")
```

## dplyr and tidyr: transform

`get_file()`, `get_dataset_file()`, `get_dataset_data()` and `run_saved_query()` return tibbles, ready for dplyr:

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

cases <- get_dataset_data("routine-data", pattern = "^cases_")

monthly <- cases |>
  group_by(district, month) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# one column per month, e.g. for a report table
monthly |> pivot_wider(names_from = month, values_from = cases)
```

## purrr: many files at once

`list_files()` and `list_dataset_files()` return tibbles too, so you can loop over their rows:

```{r}
library(purrr)

reports <- list_files("data/monthly/")
reports <- reports[grepl("\\.csv$", reports$path), ]

all_months <- map(reports$path, get_file) |> list_rbind(names_to = "file")
```

## ggplot2: static charts

Save the chart to a file, then upload it, to share it in the workspace or embed it in a report:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

chart <- ggplot(monthly, aes(month, cases, colour = district)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Monthly malaria cases", x = NULL, y = "Cases")

png <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
ggsave(png, chart, width = 8, height = 5)
upload_file(png, "outputs/charts/monthly_cases.png")
```

## plotly and leaflet: interactive web apps

`publish_webapp()` accepts any htmlwidget. A ggplot2 chart becomes interactive with `plotly::ggplotly()`:

```{r}
publish_webapp("Monthly cases", plotly::ggplotly(chart), description = "Monthly malaria cases by district")
```

A map with leaflet, from a table with coordinates:

```{r}
library(leaflet)

facilities <- get_file("data/facilities.csv") # columns: name, lat, lng, cases

map <- leaflet(facilities) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addCircleMarkers(~lng, ~lat, radius = ~ sqrt(cases), label = ~name)

publish_webapp("Facilities map", map)
```

For maps from geographic files, read them with sf through the `reader` argument:

```{r}
districts <- get_file("data/districts.geojson", reader = sf::st_read)
```

## arrow: Parquet datasets

Parquet keeps the column types and is much smaller than CSV: it is the best format for dataset files. Reading
Parquet works out of the box once arrow is installed; to write, use `arrow::write_parquet()`:

```{r}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "monthly_cases.parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(monthly, path)

create_dataset_version("malaria-indicators", "2024-12", changelog = "December extraction")
add_dataset_file("malaria-indicators", path)
```

## DBI and dbplyr: the workspace database

`connect_database()` returns a standard DBI connection. Write tables so that they can be used in the Data Studio,
in saved queries, or in dashboards connected to the database:

```{r}
con <- connect_database()

DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "monthly_cases", monthly, overwrite = TRUE)

# let the database do the work with dbplyr, then collect the result
tbl(con, "monthly_cases") |>
  filter(cases > 100) |>
  count(district) |>
  collect()

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

## R Markdown and Quarto: reports

Render a report to a self-contained HTML file, and publish it as a web app. Publishing again under the same name
updates it at the same URL:

```{r}
rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_file = "report.html", output_dir = tempdir())
publish_webapp("Monthly report", file.path(tempdir(), "report.html"), message = "December update")

# with Quarto, render to a folder and publish the whole folder (it must contain an index.html)
quarto::quarto_render("report/") # writes report/_site/
publish_webapp("Monthly report", "report/_site/")
```

## A complete flow, with data generated locally

Nothing in this flow comes from OpenHEXA: the data is simulated in R, so you can run it on any workspace where you
can write, to try the package or as a template for your own pipelines. OpenHEXA only receives the results: a
file, a dataset version, a database table, a web app and a notebook.

```{r}
library(openhexa)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)

# 1. Simulate monthly cases for a few districts, with a seasonal peak in the rainy season
districts <- tibble(
  district = c("Bobo-Dioulasso", "Ouagadougou", "Koudougou", "Banfora"),
  population = c(900000, 2500000, 160000, 120000),
  lat = c(11.18, 12.37, 12.25, 10.63),
  lng = c(-4.30, -1.52, -2.36, -4.76)
)
months <- seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-01"), by = "month")

cases <- tidyr::expand_grid(districts, month = months) |>
  mutate(
    season = 1 + 0.8 * sin((as.integer(format(month, "%m")) - 4) / 12 * 2 * pi),
    cases = rpois(n(), population / 1000 * season),
    incidence = round(cases / population * 1000, 2)
  ) |>
  select(district, month, cases, incidence, lat, lng)

current_run$log_info("Simulated ", nrow(cases), " rows") # printed in the console, or sent to the run page

# 2. Upload the raw data as a CSV file
csv <- file.path(tempdir(), "simulated_cases.csv")
readr::write_csv(cases, csv)
upload_file(csv, "simulated/simulated_cases.csv")

# 3. Publish it as a new version of a dataset, created on the first run
dataset <- tryCatch(
  get_dataset("simulated-malaria-cases"),
  openhexa_not_found_error = function(e) {
    create_dataset("Simulated malaria cases", description = "Simulated with the openhexa R package")
  }
)
parquet <- file.path(tempdir(), "cases.parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(cases, parquet)
create_dataset_version(dataset, format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"), changelog = "New simulation")
add_dataset_file(dataset, parquet)

# 4. Write a summary table to the workspace database
yearly <- cases |>
  group_by(district) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), incidence = round(sum(incidence), 1))

con <- connect_database()
DBI::dbWriteTable(con, "simulated_yearly_cases", yearly, overwrite = TRUE)
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

# 5. Publish a chart and a map as web apps
chart <- ggplot(cases, aes(month, incidence, colour = district)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Simulated malaria incidence (per 1,000)", x = NULL, y = NULL)
publish_webapp("Simulated incidence", plotly::ggplotly(chart))

map <- leaflet::leaflet(left_join(yearly, districts, by = "district")) |>
  leaflet::addTiles() |>
  leaflet::addCircleMarkers(~lng, ~lat, radius = ~ sqrt(cases) / 10, label = ~district)
publish_webapp("Simulated incidence map", map)

# 6. Create a notebook that reads the dataset back, for colleagues to explore
create_notebook("simulated/explore.ipynb", c(
  markdown = "# Simulated malaria cases",
  "library(openhexa)",
  sprintf("cases <- get_dataset_file('%s', 'cases.parquet')", dataset$slug),
  "summary(cases)"
), overwrite = TRUE)

current_run$log_info("Published the simulated data")
```

To run it on a schedule, save it as an R script and start it from a pipeline: `current_run` then sends the
messages to the run page instead of the console.
